title: The More You Spend on the Wedding, the Higher the Divorce Rate — and the Couples Who Spend Least Are the Most Stable
dek: Research shows lower wedding spending predicts lower divorce rates, with the lowest rates among those who spend under $1,000; and the more spent on an engagement ring, the higher the husband's divorce risk.
why: One episode breaks marital finance into five parts — mate selection, prenups, weddings, accounts, and decision rights — each backed by citable research, not platitudes.
who: Founders and investors who are married or about to be, especially couples where one partner runs the family finances and the other rarely takes part in decisions.
skip: The listener comments and PWL internal-event chatter at the end can be skipped.

points.h: Being a tightwad isn't saving money — it's feeling pain when you spend
points.body: The 2008 paper splits spending tendencies into tightwad and spendthrift poles, and the core variable is the "anticipatory pain of paying" — the immediate emotional reaction at the moment of purchase, not a rational calculation about the future. A tightwad feels too much pain when spending and spends less than they ideally would; a spendthrift feels too little and spends more than they ideally would. The key distinction: a frugal person derives pleasure from saving, while a tightwad suffers pain from spending. So the scale doesn't measure how much you spend but the gap between your actual behavior and your ideal self — you can be wealthy and a tightwad, or nearly bankrupt and a spendthrift.

points.h: Tightwads and spendthrifts are more likely to marry each other
points.body: Research shows tightwads are more likely to marry spendthrifts than their own kind. The authors' explanation: people have poor introspective ability about what will attract them in a real partner; when the other person displays the same spending flaw as you, it reminds you of that negative trait in yourself, so "fatal fiscal attractions" occur — someone who doesn't share your flaw is actually less attractive at first. But the excitement is short-lived: cross-pole couples report more frequent money conflicts and lower marital happiness, and the wider the gap between the two on the scale, the more likely conflict becomes. This holds even after controlling for household debt and savings.

points.h: Nobody talks about prenups because of two mechanisms
points.body: First, optimism bias: one study found engaged couples could accurately estimate the national divorce rate but estimated their own odds of divorce far below it. That creates real risk — they may sign an agreement without seriously considering the divorce scenario the agreement was designed to govern. Second, signaling cost: law-and-economics research argues that merely raising the topic of a prenup is itself a negative signal of insufficient commitment to the relationship, so partners are reluctant to bring it up first. The two mechanisms compound, leaving prenups severely underused and, where they exist, possibly hastily designed.

points.h: The more you spend on the wedding, the higher the divorce risk
points.body: The 2021 Journal of Consumer Policy paper, with survey data from more than 3,000 married respondents, found the opposite of intuition after controlling for income, demographics, and other relationship factors: the more spent on an engagement ring, the higher the husband's divorce risk; the more spent on the wedding, the higher the wife's divorce risk. Wedding-related debt stress is one possible mechanism. The couples with the lowest divorce rates spent under $1,000 on their wedding. But the same study has two counterintuitive positive findings: more guests, and taking a honeymoon (regardless of price), both predict longer marriages.

points.h: Thinking of money as shared matters more than merging accounts
points.body: A 2022 analysis spanning six studies and more than 38,000 participants found that couples who fully merged their finances had higher relationship satisfaction and were less likely to break up, and this held across cultures. A 2023 Journal of Consumer Research study found that joint accounts promote communal norms, shared goals, and a better sense of team money management. But Johanna Peets' 2025 paper "Talk About Shared Money" points out that the benefits of merging finances may not come from actually merging accounts — merely directing attention to an existing joint account rather than separate individual accounts produces similar effects. In other words, thinking of finances as "ours" rather than "mine and yours" is the step that does the work.

points.h: Financial infidelity hurts a relationship more than mismatched spending views
points.body: Financial infidelity is defined as engaging in financial behavior you expect your partner would object to and hiding it. A recent paper found that when one partner is more inclined to do this than the other, such mismatched couples are more likely to drift toward separate financial goals, predicting lower financial well-being and relationship satisfaction. This holds even after controlling for other partner mismatches (such as one tightwad and one spendthrift). Sticking to joint accounts only makes hiding large expenditures harder, but Benjamin argues it won't stop someone who really wants to hide — they'll either open another account or force the issue early, and that's beyond what financial planning can fix.

points.h: In household asset allocation, the husband's risk preference carries more weight
points.body: A 2026 Review of Financial Studies paper shows that Australian households on average incorporate only 40% of the wife's risk preference into household asset allocation, versus 60% of the husband's — a 20-percentage-point bargaining gap, the authors say; half is explained by observable characteristics like income and employment, and the other half is attributed to a gender effect. The husband's average bargaining weight is 69% in Germany and 60.1% in the US; the three countries are statistically indistinguishable but all exceed 60%. The 2021 Journal of Finance paper "Who Wears the Pants" found that US households where the husband has high financial literacy are more likely to participate in the stock market than households where the wife has equal literacy, which the authors argue is better explained by gender identity norms than by ability differences.

points.h: The biggest risk is when the partner who manages the money dies first
points.body: If one partner handles all financial decisions and the other is completely in the dark, then if the primary money manager dies or suffers cognitive decline, the survivor will have a very hard time taking over. Benjamin says they have many clients who come to them very late in life, often because the partner who always managed the money worries that their spouse won't be able to cope independently after they're gone — and "the sharks will start circling": the banks will call. He also mentions a paper from a few years ago showing that undetected cognitive decline leads to poor financial decisions, so some people use hiring an advisor as a hedge against that.
